Nike stock: Performance business offers a bright spot before Investor Day
sum: Nike's Performance business is emerging as the clearest growth opportunity ahead of the company's Investor Day, even as planned supply reductions and weak demand weigh on the broader portfolio. Trefis reported on Friday, November 13, that management expects fiscal 2027 revenue to decline at a high-single-digit rate, while Performance products continue to gain ground.

According to the Trefis analysis, the Performance business grew at a high-single-digit rate in the fiscal first quarter ended August 31, 2026. Nike's total revenue fell 4.3 percent from a year earlier during the quarter, highlighting the gap between the growing performance categories and the weaker parts of the portfolio.

Running, football, basketball and training were the main contributors to the stronger performance trend. Running grew at a double-digit rate, while Global Football posted strong double-digit growth across all four regions, according to management comments cited by Trefis. Excluding Greater China, Nike said the Performance business would have grown at a low-double-digit rate.

The business has become substantial enough to influence the group outlook. Nike said Performance reached 16 billion US dollars in fiscal 2026, compared with total company revenue of 46.4 billion US dollars. By contrast, Sportswear represented just under half of fiscal first-quarter revenue and declined at a low-double-digit rate.

Nike is scheduled to hold its 2026 Investor Day on November 16 and 17, with the main webcast listed for November 17 at 8:30 a.m. Pacific Time on the company's investor relations site. Management is expected to present portfolio priorities and its long-term growth framework.

The strategy update comes after Nike said on its October 1 earnings call that additional pressure could continue through fiscal 2027 and extend into fiscal 2028. The company's fiscal-year outlook assumes that Greater China will worsen for the remainder of fiscal 2027. Nike also expects tougher comparisons in Europe and North America to reduce second-quarter revenue growth by about 400 basis points.

Nike's latest company figures provide the operating backdrop for the event: fiscal first-quarter revenue was 11.2 billion US dollars, EBIT was 907 million US dollars and diluted earnings per share came to 0.48 US dollars.

sum: Shares of NIKE Inc. NKE have endured a steep sell-off year to date, reflecting investor concerns surrounding sluggish demand, competitive pressures and the pace of the company’s ongoing business turnaround. The steep correction has significantly reset expectations for the sportswear giant and brought its valuation into focus. While near-term headwinds continue to cloud the outlook, NIKE’s strong brand equity, strategic initiatives and efforts to reignite product innovation could support a recovery over time.
Shares of NIKE have declined 39.8% in the year-to-date period, underperforming the Shoes and Retail Apparel industry’s 33.8% fall, the broader sector’s 6.9% loss and the S&P 500 index’s 8.8% growth.

NIKE has also lagged its competitor adidas AG ADDYY, which has dropped 0.2% in the year-to-date period. NKE’s performance is notably weaker than Wolverine World Wide WWW and Steven Madden SHOO, which posted gains of 20.9% and 2.6%, respectively, in the same period.
At the current share price of $38.32, NKE trades 19.9% above its 52-week low mark of $31.9. Meanwhile, NKE stock’s price stands 45% below its 52-week high of $69.14.

NIKE's recovery remains uneven as weakness in its Sportswear business continues to overshadow gains in performance categories. Sportswear, which accounted for just under half of first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenues, declined in the low double digits. The planned reduction in Dunk revenues by nearly 50% created an approximately $200 million headwind, while disappointing sell-through of older footwear styles affected future wholesale orders. Persistent weakness in lifestyle demand remains a concern for revenue recovery.

Jordan Brand is another source of pressure, with fiscal first-quarter revenues declining in the mid-teens. Management acknowledged that the excessive supply of iconic retro footwear has weakened product scarcity and marketplace positioning. Consequently, NIKE plans to reduce the volume and frequency of selected Jordan Retro launches, particularly affecting North America. Although these actions aim to restore brand exclusivity and improve full-price sales over time, they could further constrain near-term revenues.

Higher-than-expected October inflation data pushed US Treasury yields higher and revived worries about further interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, dragging on equities across the board. Truist Securities cut its rating on the sportswear maker from "Hold" to "Sell" on Thursday, though analyst Joseph Civello left his price target unchanged at $29. The downgrade sharpened the firm's stance without touching its target, meaning the more critical view applied to the rating itself while the core reservations about the company's valuation and ongoing challenges stayed put.

Nigerians Haven’t Stopped Partying, They’re Spending Smarter – Nike Babajide
sum: In this interview with Mohammed Shosanya, the Founder and Creative Director of Atmospheric Events, Nike Babajide, shares insights into the company”s 13-year journey and how Nigeria’ economy has influenced spending on parties, weddings, and corporate events.
What gap did you see in the Lagos event decor space that made you start Atmospheric 13 years ago?

Interestingly, when I started, I didn’t necessarily identify a particular gap. I had just graduated and gone for training in event decoration and planning. I have always enjoyed organising things, but I didn’t really understand that event planning could be a profession until I attended the training. During that period, I discovered that I naturally had an interest in organisation and administration. Even while I was training, I found myself helping my trainer organise aspects of the store. At the time, event planning was not something many people around me fully understood. It was easier to sell decoration because people could see what it involved.
It is generally believed that most decor brands in Lagos don’t make it past three years. What was your toughest year?

My third year in business, around 2016, was particularly difficult. I remember having about six consecutive months without any business coming in. It was discouraging, and I genuinely began to consider whether I should continue. At some point, I started looking for paid employment while trying to keep Atmospheric running. Eventually, I got an opportunity to work in a coordination role with a planning company known for high professional standards. I was with them for about three to four years, but I never stopped running Atmospheric. That experience was very valuable. I gained more exposure, saw how other professionals worked, and learnt a lot about standards, punctuality and attention to detail.

The industry has changed significantly. When I started in 2013, many people did not fully understand why they needed a professional event planner. Decoration itself has also evolved. Back then, decoration centred around table covers, chair covers, and centrepieces. Today, it has gone far beyond that. We now pay much more attention to textures, materials, installations, styling and the overall experience guests have.

What Is Really Behind Nike Stock's Run?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Nike (NKE) is deliberately reducing some of its own sales by supplying fewer of its lifestyle shoes, and that strategy may be what Nike bulls are counting on. You probably read falling sales as a sign that shoppers are leaving Nike, but part of that decline is planned. Nike stock returned 17.0% from October 6 to November 4, 2026, though it is still down 31.7% over the past year. Part of the rise came on October 15, when Nike gained 5.2% as buyers moved into beaten-down consumer stocks and away from the AI trade. So how much of Nike's sales fall is its own choice?

Nike reduced revenue from the Dunk, part of its NIKE Sportswear business, by nearly 50% in fiscal Q1 2027 as planned. Management said this cut cost Sportswear roughly $200 million in revenue, compared to a $507 million drop in Nike's total revenue from a year earlier. That single planned reduction accounts for a large part of the quarter's drop.

The Dunk is not the only product facing reductions. Revenue for the Jordan Brand, which made up 13% of Nike's business in the quarter, fell by a mid-teens percentage, a figure management provided to demonstrate the scale of its quarterly cuts. The company also plans to reduce the volume and frequency of specific Jordan Retro launches. In Greater China, where revenue fell 26%, Nike is eliminating distribution through channels that do not fit its strategy.

Not all of the decline was intentional, however. Management said some older, high-volume Sportswear shoes sold below expectations, and noted that shoppers are cautious. So a large part of the quarter's fall is planned, with weak demand on top.

Management says the cuts will mean less deep discounting of Nike's brands and stronger full-price sales. Nike has not shown that payoff yet. Its quarterly gross margin was 42.8% in fiscal Q1 2027, up from 42.2% in fiscal Q1 2026, but management credited supply chain cost management and currency gains, which were partly offset by more discounting.
Meanwhile, Nike is not finished shrinking. Management expects fiscal 2027 revenue to decline in the high single digits, and expects EBIT, its operating profit, to fall by a greater percentage.

Why I Still Wouldn't Buy Nike Stock in November
sum: As the 2026 investing year winds down, more investors are analyzing their portfolios and preparing for 2027. For some investors, it may mean cutting positions or making sure they aren't overly concentrated in one specific area.

Others may be worried they have too many growth stocks and not enough income stocks. With Nike's (NYSE: NKE) dividend yielding a respectable 4.2%, it may seem like a good addition to a portfolio. However, a closer look reveals more considerations are needed than just yield.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

When CEO Elliott Hill, a longtime Nike veteran who joined the company in the late 1980s as a sales representative intern, took over in 2024, he had his work cut out for him. Nike had made a series of missteps over the years, ranging from shunning wholesalers to failing to keep up with changes in consumer tastes.

A finalized turnaround under Hill, however, hasn't quite happened. For its fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings, Nike reported revenue of $11.2 billion, down 4% from the prior-year period. Along with that drop in overall revenue, Nike also saw its net income decrease 2% to $712 million.

Adding more woes to the rough quarter, Nike announced a restructuring plan expected to lead to layoffs and forecast that 2027 full-year revenue will fall by a high-single-digit percentage. With the stock price down around 39% so far in 2026, there don't appear to be any immediate catalysts to reverse those losses. With that gloomy full-year 2027 sales forecast, Nike doesn't seem likely to beat analyst estimates or be in a position to boost its outlook anytime soon.

That said, as much as Nike's sales have been an issue, there's also a brewing issue of expectations that could continue to weigh on the stock. There's a perception problem with Nike, and the market still hasn't quite caught on that the iconic retailer may need to be reevaluated.

sum: Professional investors get paid a lot of money to have opinions on stocks. But an industry secret that most people may not realize is that even after exhaustive research, most stocks that professional investors look at go into the "too hard" pile.

Many individual investors may not realize this since Wall Street sell-side analysts always have "buy," "hold," and occasionally "sell" ratings on stocks. However, these are not the analysts that are paid to make actual investment decisions; that instead comes from buy-side analysts. They are the ones doing the research, helping portfolio managers construct their portfolios.

So, if you're looking for the honest answer as to whether you should buy Nike (NKE -2.45%) stock for the long haul, the truthful answer is that the apparel stock squarely falls into the "too hard" pile.

Nike is an iconic brand known throughout the world. Its swoosh logo and "Just Do It" slogan have given the company brand equity that most consumer companies dream of. However, it is also a struggling brand trying to recover from years of missteps under its former CEO.

When Nike named John Donahoe as CEO in 2020, it brought in a tech-savvy leader who had helmed both eBay and software giant ServiceNow. However, he had no brand experience and turned his attention to creating a higher-margin business. He de-emphasized product innovation (shifting R&D investments to digital infrastructure) in favor of riding the company's classic shoe businesses, like the Jordan brand, and shunned the wholesale channel to focus on its higher-margin direct-to-consumer (DTC) business. The result was a disaster that Nike's new CEO is still working to fix.

However, a lot of damage has been done. By cutting ties with long-term retail partners, Nike lost out on space to brands like Hoka, owned by Deckers, and On Running. Meanwhile, competitors caught up with technology, and Nike's classic footwear business became oversaturated. The damage was particularly acute in China as local brands like Anta and Li-Ning emerged, and Nike wasn't meeting consumers where they shop with its DTC strategy.
Nike has the potential to turn around its business, but it's not an easy process, and tariffs and a trade war with China made things even more difficult.

Nike Stock Forecast 2030: The Underestimated Best Brand on Earth
sum: Nike’s biggest mistake was trying to become a digital platform. The unwind is painful, intentional, and exactly why the brand is setting up for a premium re-rating by 2030.

Nike enters this cycle burdened by the perception that its best years are behind it. Revenue volatility, margin compression, and a prolonged drawdown in digital performance have combined to produce a narrative of structural decline. That narrative mistakes transition costs for terminal weakness.

Our view is narrower and more mechanical. Nike did not lose brand relevance. It misallocated power within its operating system by prioritizing direct digital control over the wholesale ecosystem that historically scaled its brand, its volume, and its cultural presence. The consequences of that decision are now visible in shrinking digital revenue, strained partner relationships, and near-term margin pressure. The market is interpreting these outcomes as evidence of deterioration. We interpret them as evidence of correction.

The central claim of this forecast is simple. Nike’s attempt to become a digital platform was a strategic error. The unwind of that strategy is not a retreat. It is the prerequisite for stabilization. As digital exposure is reduced, wholesale relationships are repaired, inventory discipline returns, and capital allocation regains coherence, Nike’s core business begins to look structurally stronger, not weaker.

We do not assume a rapid rebound. The path through stabilization is uneven by design. Growth remains muted in the near term as the system rebalances. Offense follows only after repair is complete. Under experienced leadership, we expect Nike to re-enter a phase of modest but durable growth, supported by cleaner supply chains, a refocused product portfolio, and a global brand whose pricing power the market continues to undervalue.

By 2030, our base case reflects a Nike that is no longer attempting to dominate distribution, but one that has reasserted control over execution. Revenue growth reaccelerates to 6%, operating margins normalize toward mid-teens levels, free cash flow scales meaningfully, and a premium valuation multiple becomes justified once again. The opportunity is not in calling the bottom. It is in recognizing that the unwind itself is the inflection.
